<description>
{
 "summary": "Adds structural descriptor inspection and multisig safety analysis to Bitcoin Core, exposed via a new `analyzedescriptor` wallet RPC and a `verbose` flag on `getdescriptorinfo`. Core reconstructs key inventories and policy trees to verify whether an output descriptor matches a recognized k-of-n multisig configuration without hidden spend paths or duplicate cosigner keys. The wallet RPC correlates descriptor keys with the loaded wallet to determine cosigner ownership, reports whether the wallet can sign, and computes the first receive address.",
 "problem": "When joining a multisig setup, participants must verify that a coordinator-supplied descriptor adheres strictly to their agreed k-of-n policy, contains their key, and generates identical addresses. Core currently does not report what spending policies a descriptor commits to, requiring external tools to parse descriptor strings manually and risking vulnerabilities like repeated keys that lower effective signing thresholds.",
 "evidence": [
  "PR description: \"Before importing a multisig descriptor received from a coordinator, each participant needs to check that it is the setup they agreed on: a k-of-n where any k cosigners can spend and nothing else can, that their own key is in it, and that they all derived the same first address. Today nothing in Core reports what a descriptor commits to, so tools had to parse the descriptor string by hand, as the multisig wizard in #36325 (now closed) did.\"",
  "Commit e14990c876: \"Two cosigner slots are the same holder if they share a root key, or derive the same key at the first address (an xpub and its own child). Core accepts such descriptors, and fewer signers than the threshold can spend from them.\""
 ],

<category name="ipc" title="IPC / multiprocess">
## Covers

The process-separation project and everything that serves it: the
`interfaces::` abstraction layer between node, wallet, and GUI, the Cap'n
Proto interface definitions and generated-code machinery, the
libmultiprocess subtree, the `bitcoin-node` / `bitcoin-gui` /
`bitcoin-wallet` executables and the `bitcoin` wrapper, IPC process
management (spawning, connecting, disconnect handling), and the tests and
build glue for all of it. The IPC label is a strong prior.

Not ipc: PRs whose subject is what the mining interface exposes or how
templates are built (category `mining`), even though they travel over
IPC. A mining PR is ipc only if it changes IPC infrastructure itself
(serialization, connection handling, the capnp toolchain). Likewise a
wallet or GUI PR that adds a method to `interfaces::Wallet` is wallet
first; it is ipc only if the interface mechanics are the point.

A general-utility PR (a result type, a logging helper) that the
multiprocess stack happens to be based on is not ipc.

## What matters here

Anything that lets external software use the node over IPC reliably: the
stability and completeness of the mining interface and its consumers,
crash and disconnect handling, correctness of serialization across the
process boundary, and platform coverage (the IPC binaries building and
passing tests on every supported platform). Then progress on running the
wallet and GUI as separate processes, which is the project's stated goal.
Then reductions in the maintenance burden of the interface layer:
generated code, build integration, the libmultiprocess subtree sync.

Interface cleanups without a consumer waiting on them are P3 or below.

hint matches: {"keywords": ["interfaces::"], "paths": ["src/interfaces/wallet.h"]}
</category>

<category name="rpc" title="RPC / REST / ZMQ">
## Covers

The node's programmatic interfaces: JSON-RPC methods and their help and
argument handling, the HTTP server and authentication, `bitcoin-cli`,
the REST interface, and ZMQ notifications. Wallet RPCs are wallet first
and rpc second unless the change is to the RPC machinery itself. The
RPC/REST/ZMQ label is a strong prior.

Not rpc: the behavior an RPC merely exposes (that belongs to its area).

## What matters here

Compatibility first: changes that break or silently alter what existing
callers get back affect every application built on the node, so
correctness of returned data and the discipline around deprecations
matter most. Then security of the interface: authentication, exposure
of sensitive data, resource exhaustion through the HTTP server. Then
gaps that force applications into workarounds: missing fields or
methods that downstream software has asked for, with evidence they
asked. Then performance of hot methods that block explorers and
indexers call constantly. Then consistency and documentation of the
interface.

New methods without an external consumer asking rank low.

hint matches: {"keywords": ["rpc", "bitcoin-cli", "REST", "json", "-rpc"], "paths": ["src/rpc/client.cpp", "src/rpc/descriptor_util.cpp", "src/rpc/descriptor_util.h", "src/rpc/output_script.cpp", "test/functional/rpc_getdescriptorinfo.py"]}
</category>

<category name="tests" title="Test infrastructure">
## Covers

The machinery of testing rather than tests of a particular area: the
functional test framework and runner, unit test utilities, the fuzzing
harnesses and corpora, benchmarks, linters, sanitizer configuration,
and fixes for flaky tests whose cause is in the framework. A test that
pins the behavior of one area (a wallet migration test, a p2p relay
test) belongs to that area, not here. The Tests and Fuzzing labels are
a prior, but a labeled PR whose tests are about one area goes to that
area instead.

## What matters here

Signal first: fixes for flaky or misleading tests, since a red CI that
nobody trusts hides real failures. Then coverage of high-risk code paths
that the fuzzers or functional tests do not reach, especially
consensus, mempool policy, and p2p message handling. Then framework
capabilities that unblock tests other areas need. Then test speed, which
every contributor pays for on every run. Then cleanliness of the test
code.

Adding tests for their own sake ranks low; adding a test that catches a
realistic regression ranks high.

hint matches: {"keywords": ["fuzz"], "paths": ["src/test/fuzz/descriptor_parse.cpp", "test/functional/test_runner.py"]}
</category>

<category name="wallet" title="Wallet">
## Covers

The bitcoind wallet: key and descriptor management, transaction creation
and coin selection, PSBT handling, wallet database (SQLite, and the
legacy BDB migration path), backup and recovery, rescanning, wallet RPCs,
and wallet-facing pieces of the GUI. Fee estimation is wallet when the
change is about how the wallet uses it.

Borderline: a descriptor or PSBT change that affects only `bitcoin-tx` or
RPC without wallet code is rpc, not wallet. An `interfaces::Wallet`
change is both wallet and ipc.

## What matters here

Fund safety first: anything that could lose keys, double-spend
unintentionally, create an unspendable output, or corrupt the wallet
database. Then backup, recovery, and migration correctness, including the
legacy-to-descriptor migration path that every remaining legacy user
must cross. Then privacy of transaction creation (address reuse, change
detection, fingerprinting). Then user-visible reliability: hangs, slow
rescans, confusing failures, wrong balances. Then features users have
asked for, with evidence they have asked.

The rubric does not ask whether Bitcoin Core should have a wallet. It
asks, given that it does, what a wallet user needs most.
